archetype.name: Game Manager (mobile backup)
archetype.definition: A short-area, low-risk distributor who keeps the Ravens' offense on schedule with quick completions, zero turnovers and designed runs, rather than driving the ball downfield.

report.headline: Turnover-free and efficient enough, but his ceiling is capped by short throws and sacks
report.take:
Huntley is doing what he has done in every Baltimore stint. He completes a lot of passes, rarely puts the ball in danger and gives the offense a designed-run element. He doesn't push the ball. His 70.8% completion rate ranks 5th of 45 and he has no interceptions, but his 5.96 yards per attempt ranks 36th. His intended air yards of 6.69 sit about two yards short of the sticks. That yards-per-attempt figure is a career constant: 5.75, 5.88, 5.49, 6.23 and 6.36 across his past seasons. This is his profile, not a slump.

The efficiency that does show up comes from a small set of throws. His 53 attempts under 10 air yards are net negative (-0.014 EPA a play). His 19 throws of 10+ yards produce +0.544 a play and nearly all of his passing value. Nine red-zone plays at +0.853 with three touchdowns add more. Both are thin samples, and the deep and intermediate numbers come with completion rates under expectation, so the payoff there is lumpy rather than repeatable. The NGS tracking CPOE of -2.49 also cuts against the box-score +4.52. Much of the completion rate is simply what short throws are supposed to produce.

The cost sits in the pocket. Huntley is barely pressured (10.7%, 2nd lowest), and his 4.2% bad-throw rate is the best among charted qualifiers. But when pressure arrives, 37.5% of it becomes a sack, 33rd of 37. His career pressure-to-sack marks run from 0.36 to 0.42, so this is a durable trait of a smaller QB who holds the ball looking for a lane. It is the main reason his total dropback EPA (1.3) is so much lower than his passing EPA (8.3). The target tree matters too. Mark Andrews has been a black hole with him at -1.028 EPA per target, while Josh Cuevas and Rashod Bateman have carried the passing game.

Where it's heading depends less on Huntley than on Lamar Jackson's ankle. Jackson is listed Out but day-to-day and could practice this week. If Huntley starts, expect the same thing: around 180 passing yards, a rushing floor, and a low-mistake operation that wins when the defense and run game hold up.

strengths.title: Ball security and clean throws
strengths.body: He has no interceptions on 72 attempts and the lowest bad-throw rate among charted qualifiers. That fits his career pattern of high completion rates and his 0-interception 2025. Some of it is short-throw selection, but it is a real, repeatable skill that keeps the Ravens out of bad game scripts.

strengths.title: Designed-run value
strengths.body: Called runs have been his most efficient plays: +0.471 EPA, an 80% success rate and a touchdown on five tries. His 21.3 rushing yards a game rank 15th, and he has put up 100-plus rushing yards in multiple seasons. That gives him a fantasy and red-zone floor that does not depend on the passing game.

strengths.title: Finishing in the red zone
strengths.body: Nine red-zone plays have produced three touchdowns at +0.853 EPA a play. This is a small sample that will cool off, but it fits a QB who can threaten with his legs near the goal line.

concerns.title: Short passing that doesn't gain yards
concerns.body: His sub-10-yard throws, nearly three-quarters of his attempts, are net negative. Screens and throws behind the line lose value (-0.101 a play). Low yards per attempt has followed him for five seasons, so expect it to continue. It caps how much offense he can carry when the run game stalls.

concerns.title: Pressure turns into sacks
concerns.body: He is rarely pressured, yet 37.5% of the pressure he does face ends in a sack, one of the worst rates in the league. His career rates have always sat in this range. It comes from holding the ball to extend plays, and his scrambles (+0.033 EPA, no first downs) haven't paid for it.

concerns.title: Efficiency rests on a few throws
concerns.body: Almost all of his passing value comes from 19 attempts of 10+ air yards, completed under expectation. A handful of big gains can flip from positive to negative quickly. The Andrews connection (-1.028 per target) is also dragging the whole passing line down.

trend.note: In two starts, the Atlanta game was more efficient on short throws (24/32, 2 TD), while Cleveland saw him push the ball further (intended air yards 4.8 to 8.7) for a better passing EPA but fewer yards. He took three sacks in each start, so the shape of the game hasn't really changed.

nextGame.headline: Cincinnati gives up short throws and runs, but gets sacks
nextGame.body:
Cincinnati's defense lines up with Huntley's profile in mixed ways. It is leaky underneath (29th in short-pass EPA) and soft against the run (28th in rush EPA, 30th in explosive runs allowed), which suits a short-area passer with designed runs. But it is 5th against deep passes and 3rd in sack rate, which hits his worst trait directly. The Bengals' offense is the league's most pass-heavy in neutral situations, and a 51.5 total with Baltimore favored by 2.5 points to a game with more possessions than his first two starts.

Availability frames everything. Lamar Jackson is Out but day-to-day and could practice. If Jackson returns, Huntley goes back to the bench and this outlook doesn't apply. Center Cam Jurgens (concussion) is Out after playing every snap this season, and a backup center against a top-3 sack defense is a real problem for a QB who turns pressure into sacks. Bateman is expected to be OK, which matters because he and Cuevas have been Huntley's productive targets, with fellow tight end Hibner out. Cincinnati losing backup TE Tanner Hudson doesn't affect this matchup.

keyMatchups.title: Sack rate against a fill-in center
keyMatchups.body: Cincinnati is 3rd in sack rate, and Huntley converts pressure to sacks at one of the league's worst rates. With Jurgens out, interior pressure is the most likely way his drives die. Quick, short timing throws are his best defense.

keyMatchups.title: Soft underneath coverage
keyMatchups.body: The Bengals allow +0.221 EPA on short passes, 29th in the league, exactly where Huntley throws most. This is the matchup that could make his low-air-yard game actually move the ball, instead of netting negative as it has so far.

keyMatchups.title: Run game and QB keepers
keyMatchups.body: Cincinnati ranks 28th against the run and 30th in explosive runs allowed. That helps Baltimore's ground game and Huntley's designed runs, and keeps games on schedule for a QB who struggles in long-yardage dropbacks.

nextGame.watch: Jackson's practice reports during the week: if he is a full participant, Huntley's start is off.

restOfSeason.body: Huntley's role ends when Jackson's ankle allows, and the coach has called Jackson day-to-day. So the realistic rest-of-season picture is a few more spot starts at most, then backup duty. The ranges below are for the games he starts. In those, expect what five seasons of data say he is: a high completion rate, a yards-per-attempt figure around 6, few or no interceptions, two or three sacks a game, and steady rushing value. The 0% interception rate and the red-zone touchdown rate will regress; the low-air-yard, sack-prone shape won't.
swingFactors: Lamar Jackson's ankle and return timing
Whether Andrews' targets keep failing or shift to Bateman and Cuevas

confidence.note: 72 attempts, two starts, and his playing time depends on Jackson's health week to week.
